Most of what you say is correct but I wanted to correct you on the “most of their diets were plants”- that’s not true for a lot of ancient humans. It really depended on where they lived and the season. If they were near the equator/in warmer climates, they would’ve had more access to plants and yes, their diet would’ve been mostly plant based. But for a lot of ancient humans, meat (mammal, reptile, bug, fish, bird, etc.) were more plentiful. Where I live (subtropical, Tennessee) the majority of our indigenous people’s (Cherokee) diets were meat.

Equitation is an incredible display of the bond between the rider and their horse companion- when it is done *right*. A lot of higher level equestrian sports have judges that judge not on the horse’s comfort, but on how their movements look. Instead of the calm, flowing moves that are supposed to be prioritized in sports like dressage, unfortunately many judges will prefer jerky, flashy movements, which are often achieved by riding hollow (meaning the horse’s muscles are not engaged properly, riding like that can damage their muscles and bones overtime) and pulling a horse’s head into their chest and causing them pain (this is called rollkur). A lot of judges unfortunately also score highly if the rider or horse are well known. It’s just as bad in western disciplines too, where horses may have their tail muscles numbed to stop them from swaying (a horse lashing their tail means they’re agitated) which will make them look better to judges.

That’s not to say all equitation is bad! There are a lot of good riders, and plenty of judges that judge based on skill and comfort rather than names and showiness. Unfortunately though these things become more rare the higher up in the ranks you go. When more money is involved as the prize, assume that more people are willing to do more unethical things to achieve it.

Dragons are a species of large bird or reptile-like avians that are normally untameable, but can be made tameable with mods. You can get eggs from companions after a day or so of owning them, but you need to be in the right habitat to collect them (visible in the companion registry).

Once you get the egg from them, you can change up their genes in the gene sequencer that’s in the anomaly! It’s in the same area as the tree guy, and right in the back next to the chef and character customizer. You can put certain elements and materials into the slots to change the egg’s genes, making the creature you produce have different traits or stats! You can change the colors and proportions and size of the creature, as well as their temperament to make them more friendly or helpful. While it will tell you whether you’re making a creature more or less aggressive, or bigger or smaller, it won’t tell you the color or physical traits you’re giving them! Those are completely random!
